newsitem.title: BELARUS: Lukashenko confident as polls close in Belarus.
newsitem.headline: Lukashenko confident as polls close in Belarus.

text.p: Hardline Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko was confident of victory as voting ended on Sunday in a controversial referendum on extending his powers.
With turnout figures indicating a high poll in the former Soviet republic, he dropped his usual anti-Western rhetoric and appeared in conciliatory mood as he cast his ballot.
"I really respect the West and it really loves me -- as much as it is able to," he told Reuters after voting to extend his term beyond 2000 and tighten his grip on parliament.
"Apart from political rhetoric, there are no difficulties with the West," he added after talking to reporters.

Lukashenko's policies have drawn widespread criticism from Western human rights organisations and international lending bodies have withdrawn funding pending faster reforms, and the conduct of the voting has also attracted criticism.
Polling stations opened at 6 a.m. (0400 GMT) and closed at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT) on the last day of a long process that began on November 9.
By 6 p.m. (1600 GMT) 59.5 percent of the electorate -- 4,237,076 people -- had voted, the central electoral commission said, suggesting the final turnout might approach 80 percent.
Preliminary results should be available on Monday, officials say. Lukashenko is to hold a news conference at 11 a.m. (0900 GMT) on Monday.

Several hundred people demonstrated in Minsk against Lukashenko on polling day but the capital was otherwise calm, reflecting Lukashenko's control over the security apparatus and the lack of strong opposition leadership.

The heavy poll was expected to favour Lukashenko, who enjoys especially strong support in country areas of the largely-rural republic of 10 million bordering Russia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Ukraine.
The political crisis deepened on Saturday when Lukashenko and parliament both reneged on a deal brokered by neighbouring Russia aimed at resolving their dispute over the referendum.
Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin expressed "deep regret" on Sunday over the collapse of the compromise he arranged and blamed some legislators for wrecking the truce.
But the Russian premier told Itar-Tass news agency that Lukashenko could also have done more to make it succeed.
The tall, angular, moustachioed Lukashenko was in conciliatory mood on Sunday about his opponents in parliament, who have been trying to remove him from office by impeachment.
"The new constitution allows me to dissolve parliament after a month if we do not reach agreement," he said, but added: "I will not dissolve it because we will find harmony."
If his draft is approved at the polls, the constitution will be changed to create an upper house of parliament of 64 representatives and a lower house of 110 deputies.
A Council of Europe analysis said of the constitutional draft: "The interference of the President in the sphere of other state bodies could not be stronger".

He will seek approval from two-thirds of the existing parliament to form the two chambers from it. But if deputies cannot reach agreement on this within one month, he will have the right to dissolve parliament and call new elections.

Parliamentary speaker Semyon Sharetsky, who signed the agreement, said after casting his ballot that he had again been denied access to state television which backs the president and has been feeding the population a daily diet of propaganda.
"This speaks volumes about what awaits us if, God forbid, the presidential draft becomes the constitution," he said.
He warned on Saturday that tensions were growing in Belarus and accused Lukashenko of trying to "grab more power by anti- constitutional means".
Sharetsky, the main opposition figure in Belarus, has compared Lukashenko to Germany's Adolf Hitler, Italy's Benito Mussolini and Spain's Francisco Franco.

Lukashenko himself has been quoted praising Hitler. Late on Saturday, Russian ORT television broadcast a soundtrack of his voice over pictures of Auschwitz concentration camp saying Hitler brought order and stability to pre-war Germany.

But he told reporters on Sunday: "It was a falsification, an edited track. It wasn't made by journalists. You know my policies, you know my approach, and my judgements about fascism in general. I never said this. Never."
Lukashenko also said Belarus would finally send the last of its former Soviet nuclear missiles to Russia on Tuesday.
The referendum poses seven questions, including whether to accept Lukashenko's draft constitution to broaden his powers.
Lukashenko, defying parliament, the constitutional court and the Russia-brokered agreement, has decreed the referendum will be legally binding rather than advisory.
